prompt: I'm trying to show which job families are driving attrition. Can you give me 5 options I could pop into this exec's deck right now to fit this storyline?

options.headline: Pharmacy technicians and distribution center associates lose about 1 in 4 people a year, well above the 19.9% enterprise rate
options.subtitle: Voluntary attrition by job family, FY26 (%)
options.why: The classic: ranks every family and shows the two clearly above the enterprise line, so the 'who' is instant

options.chart_type: Deviation dot plot vs. enterprise rate
options.headline: Only two job families run above the 19.9% enterprise rate, by 7.5 and 4.2 points
options.subtitle: Voluntary attrition by job family vs. the enterprise rate, FY26 (%; gap in percentage points)
options.why: Turns the benchmark into the axis of the story: everyone else sits below the line, only two families sit above it

options.headline: Pharmacy technician attrition fell 5.6 points in FY26, but distribution center associates barely moved at 24.1%
options.subtitle: Voluntary attrition, FY25 vs. FY26, 6 tracked job families (%)
options.why: Adds the 'so what next': one driver is improving fast, the other is stuck, which points the exec at DC associates

options.headline: The two largest frontline job families combine attrition above 24% with the lowest engagement scores (66 and 68)
options.subtitle: Workforce scorecard by job family, FY26; totals weighted by headcount
options.why: For the exec who asks 'why': shows the two attrition drivers are also the biggest populations with the weakest engagement

options.headline: Two job families account for 73% of voluntary exits but only 58% of headcount
options.subtitle: Share of voluntary exits and of headcount, two highest-attrition job families, FY26 (%)
options.why: One number an exec remembers: nearly three-quarters of the exit problem sits in two families
